summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of the Mississippi River, the chief river of the second-largest drainage system in North America. It describes the river's course from Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico, its length of 2,320 miles, and the 31 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces its watershed drains. It also covers the basin's size, its relation to the Ohio River at Cairo, Illinois, and the states the river borders or passes through.
one_line: Overview of the Mississippi River, its 2,320-mile course from Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico, and its vast drainage basin.
key_facts: The Mississippi River is the chief river of the second-largest drainage system on the North American continent, second only to the Hudson Bay drainage system.
The river flows entirely within the United States, although its drainage basin reaches into Canada.
The river rises at Lake Itasca in northern Minnesota and flows generally south for 2,320 miles (3,730 km) to the Mississippi River Delta in the Gulf of Mexico.
The Mississippi's watershed drains all or parts of 31 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces between the Rocky and Appalachian Mountains.
The Mississippi ranks as the fourth-longest and fifteenth-largest river in the world by discharge.
The river borders or passes through the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa, Illinois, Missouri, Kentucky, Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Louisiana.
The Mississippi River has the world's fourth-largest drainage basin, covering more than 1,245,000 square miles (3,220,000 km).
The total catchment of the Mississippi River covers nearly 40% of the landmass of the continental United States.
The highest point within the watershed is Mount Elbert, at 14,440 feet (4,400 m), which is also the highest point of the Rocky Mountains.
The Mississippi River is called the Lower Mississippi River from its confluence with the Ohio River to its mouth at the Gulf of Mexico, a distance of about 1,000 miles (1,600 km).
The long-term mean discharge of the Ohio at Cairo, Illinois is 281,500 cubic feet per second (7,970 cubic metres per second).
The long-term mean discharge of the Mississippi at Thebes, Illinois (just upriver from Cairo) is 208,200 cubic feet per second (5,900 cubic metres per second).
By volume, the main branch of the Mississippi River system at Cairo can be considered to be the Ohio River (and the Allegheny River further upstream), rather than the Middle Mississippi.
